I have farmed these fields in Quzhou County my whole life. I am 72 years old now, and though I never went to school, I know this land and its seasons better than any book could teach me. Around here, the only sensible way to farm is the wheat-maize rotation — winter wheat planted in the autumn and harvested in early summer, followed immediately by summer maize. I still manage about 4 mu of good flat land myself. My son helps me arrange the machinery, but I make the decisions.

For the wheat that is already in the ground from last autumn, I will apply a topdressing of urea when it greens up in the spring, and I will irrigate it three more times after the winter irrigation I already gave it: once at jointing, once at heading, and once during grain filling. I will spray for weeds once, for insects twice, and for fungus once if the weather turns damp. Before planting the wheat last year, I rotavated the soil, which is what we always do here.

For the summer maize that I will plant right after the wheat harvest in June, I will use a hybrid variety — everyone here uses hybrid maize now because the yields are much better than the old types. I will drill the seeds directly into the wheat stubble without ploughing again; no-tillage saves time and labor, and the crop grows just fine. I will fertilize with compound fertilizer at planting and topdress with urea at the big喇叭口 stage. I will irrigate twice, and I will spray for weeds once and for corn borers twice.

This is the system that has fed my family for decades. The prices are stable, the buyers come to the village, and I have the experience to manage it without taking unnecessary risks at my age.
